The following is a faithful transcription of printed article, writ- ten by the Servant of God, Father Solanus Casey and printed in the "Irish World" C. 1922 ( He signed his name on the newsprint copy)
DISTINGUISHED MISSIONARY PRIEST DISCUSSES IRISH AMERICAN SITUATION (Editor's Headline)
Editor, The Irish World:
Rather than find bitterness in the Irish World concerning the folder recently sent out purporting to be a "statement by Right Rev. Michael J. Gallagher, D.D. dealing with the visit to the United States of Hon. Eamon DeValera," a copy which I have been assured duly reached your office, I want to congratulate you on the digni- fied silence (or prudent oversight) which in this case especially be- comes your long experience and your really responsible position.
I do not like to believe that said statement "is really and ex- pression, carefully considered, of a Bishop whom in more than one way I have admired, and who undoubtedly loves Ireland and justice. Pos- sibly, however, he has been beguiled and I deceive myself, as it seems now that I die deceive myself about 10 months ago when speaking about Cohalan's unfortunate break with DeValera, then recently made manifest, I asked you, "let us hope that his motives are not so unworthy." Per- haps a little time and honest criticism of the "statement will bring out other views and other expressions from Bishop Gallagher. For my part, I cannot think of going into details about it at this time, being as you know only a simple religious and therefore, not experienced in and not inclined to analyse such documents.
This much, however, I will say in its favor: If "differences a- rise between honest lovers of a common cause mostly because of misun- derstandings," then, whatever the motive for publishing the personal correspondence as therein given between DeValera and his opponents, the author has wittingly or unwittingly taken a positive step in the direction of settling differences between Ireland, in her representa- tive, and those in America who honestly oppose the same representative, De Valera.
Personally, at least, if I had never followed up the Irish ques- tion at all, as I certainly have been and am, I would be inclined to ask, on reading DeValera's message and the reply it occasioned - to say nothing of the two pages signed "J. D." -- I would be more than inclined to ask: "Is this the Friendship that joins the F.O. I.F. and martyred Ireland? Does not DeValera's sentence after sentence show at once a disappointed confidence and a depressed hope as well as a determination forced almost to desperation?" -- which determination opponents of Ire- land seem to mistake for unbending pride: though even the bitterest of
